Series::logaddexp2¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::logaddexp2(const Series& other) const -> Series
Series& Series::logaddexp2_(const Series& other)

What It Does¶

logaddexp2() computes log2(2^a + 2^b) elementwise — the base-2 counterpart of logaddexp().

It is the stable evaluation of that expression. The naive (a.exp2() + b.exp2()).log2() overflows as soon as a or b is a few thousand, so logaddexp2() factors out the larger operand:

m = max(a, b)
result = m + log2(1 + 2^(-|a - b|))
       = m + log1p(2^(-|a - b|)) / ln 2

Base 2 is the natural choice when your quantities are measured in bits — log2 probabilities, entropy in bits, or anything downstream of a base-2 logarithm. For everything phrased in nats, use logaddexp() instead.

Parameters¶

other (const Series&)

The second operand b. Broadcasts against the receiver.

Returns¶

Series or Series& The elementwise stable log2(2^a + 2^b). logaddexp2_() writes the result back into the receiver. Floating-point inputs only.

Gradient¶

logaddexp2() is differentiable. The backward is a base-2 softmax weight:

d/da logaddexp2(a, b) = 2^a / (2^a + 2^b) = sigmoid((a - b) * ln 2)
d/db logaddexp2(a, b) = sigmoid((b - a) * ln 2)

As with logaddexp() the two gradients sum to 1, and at a == b they split 0.5 / 0.5.

Examples¶

Example 1. logaddexp2(x, x) = x + 1, because 2^x + 2^x = 2^(x+1).

auto a = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 3.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({0.0, 2.0, 3.0});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.logaddexp2(b));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 2.5850, 4.0000]

Entry 0 is 0 + 1. Entry 1 is log2(2 + 4) = log2 6 = 2.5850. Entry 2 is 3 + 1.

Example 2. Stability: the naive base-2 form overflows here, logaddexp2() does not.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({1000.0}).logaddexp2(pluss::make_series({1000.0})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[1001.0000]

Example 3. The backward is the base-2 softmax weight and sums to 1.

auto a = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({2.0, 2.0, 1.0});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
b.tracks_slope_(true);

a.logaddexp2(b).sum().reverse();

std::cout << "da=" << a.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "db=" << b.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

da=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.33333333, 0.5, 0.8]
db=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.66666667, 0.5, 0.2]

For a - b = -1, the weight on a is 2^-1 / (2^-1 + 1) = 1/3. At a == b it is 0.5. For a - b = 2, it is 4 / (4 + 1) = 0.8.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Prefer logaddexp2() over (a.exp2() + b.exp2()).log2() whenever the operands can be large.

  • Floating-point inputs only.

  • +inf makes the result +inf; two -inf operands give -inf; NaN propagates.

  • Base 2, not base e. Mixing this up with logaddexp() rescales the result by ln 2.

Summary¶

logaddexp2(a, b) is a stable log2(2^a + 2^b):

  • broadcasts like add(); floating point only

  • built on m + log1p(2^(-|a - b|)) / ln 2

  • differentiable, gradients sigmoid((a - b) * ln 2) and its mirror, summing to 1

See Also¶

  • Series::logaddexp: the natural-log version; use it for quantities in nats.

  • Series::sigmoid: the shape of the backward weight.
